title: Reliable instruction-following physical work in unfamiliar everyday environments

concept.text: The proposed innovation is a robot system that takes an ordinary-language goal and reliably finishes an unfamiliar, multi-step physical job in an everyday environment the developers did not instrument. It would work without per-task fine-tuning, human coaching, or resets between steps. The capability includes interpreting the goal, choosing and sequencing actions, tracking how its actions change the scene, recognizing mistakes, and recovering until the specified job is finished.

One unchanged policy system could contain a fixed hierarchy of planners, reasoning models, perception systems, and motor controllers. The requirement concerns the competence of the complete system; it does not require a single monolithic neural controller. Its defining advance would be dependable completion of unfamiliar jobs within its physical capabilities, rather than success at isolated movements or separately prompted steps.

significance.text: If achieved, this capability would make physical skills reusable through instructions, reducing the programming, task-specific training, and supervision needed to put a robot to work. The supplied research already reports instruction-mediated manipulation and transfer between settings or embodiments. Extending those components to reliable whole-job completion would change the practical unit of interaction from directing individual actions to specifying an outcome. The analogy with reusable computation is a reasoned assessment of the proposed breakthrough, not a demonstrated equivalence.

As a conditional consequence, robots could perform unfamiliar jobs within their demonstrated manipulation and environment scope. Tidying, machine tending, packing, and light assembly are potential applications, especially where existing grippers or simple hands already provide adequate physical capability. A successful home evaluation would support claims about the tested home activities; extending the result to workplaces, different materials, or more demanding equipment would require additional validation. A finite set of successful jobs would establish demonstrated breadth, not universal physical competence.

Practical deployment would still depend on cost, battery endurance, maintenance, and safe interaction with people. Reliable task completion would not itself establish human-level hand dexterity or safety certification. The supplied review identifies a separate Gemini Robotics 2 safety report dated 29 July 2026 whose evaluation excludes the underlying functional safety architecture, reinforcing the distinction between demonstrated competence and a complete case for safe physical deployment.

missing_breakthrough.text: The target is dependable composition of physical skills into unfamiliar jobs without task-specific adaptation or coaching. The supplied sources report substantial components of this capability, but do not establish its full proposed scope. In particular, the π0.7 account distinguishes following unfamiliar instructions from autonomously completing some unfamiliar longer tasks: for those tasks, step-by-step coaching supplies data used to train a high-level language policy. Gemini Robotics 2 reports multi-step execution and self-correction, but the supplied account does not establish the proposed independent, shift-length evaluation.

As an engineering synthesis, a central difficulty is compositional generalization under physical interaction. A system must connect language to the actual objects and their states, order actions around dependencies, and update its plan when contact, clutter, or its own movements alter the scene. Opening an articulated appliance, manipulating a deformable object, and recovering from an unsuccessful grasp require different forms of state estimation and control. These are interacting barriers, not an experimentally established explanation of a single bottleneck.

Another engineering requirement is maintaining reliability across an entire job. Correctly following several individual instructions does not establish that all necessary steps will succeed together, that the intended outcome will be recognized, or that failures will be repaired without help. Evaluation must therefore distinguish component accuracy from whole-job success and autonomous recovery. It must also characterize task novelty: the π0.7 authors acknowledge difficulty quantifying how novel their test instructions are, which limits conclusions about generalization.

current_state.text: Physical Intelligence and colleagues report π0.7 in the arXiv preprint arXiv:2604.15483v2, revised 24 April 2026. According to the supplied review, it follows instructions in unseen kitchens and bedrooms and transfers laundry folding to a target robot without laundry-folding data from that embodiment. That result concerns transfer across embodiments; it does not mean the overall system had no laundry-training experience. The paper also reports performance competitive with specialist policies on espresso-making, laundry, and box-building without task-specific post-training of the generalist. Those comparison tasks were represented in training, including specialist rollout data, so these comparisons do not establish performance on wholly unseen jobs.

The supplied review of Figure 9's caption records sequences of 3–6 open-ended instructions across four unseen kitchens and two unseen bedrooms. The reported metric is the percentage of instructions correctly followed, rather than whole-job success over an extended work period. All tested manipulators use parallel-jaw grippers, and the authors state that instruction novelty is difficult to quantify. For some unfamiliar longer tasks, including toasting a bagel, step-by-step coaching is followed by training a high-level language policy for subsequent autonomous execution. These results support instruction following, transfer, and some multi-step execution, while preserving an important distinction between an unchanged system completing a new job and a system gaining that capability through coaching-derived training.

Carolina Parada's Google DeepMind article, dated 30 July 2026, reports that Gemini Robotics 2 uses the same vision-language-action checkpoint across several embodiments, including humanoid whole-body control spanning walking and manipulation. A separate embodied reasoning model supports task sequences lasting several minutes and involving hundreds of decisions, with reported self-correction when a step fails. The article also states that multi-finger dexterous manipulation remains challenging. Its adaptation claim applies specifically to the On-Device 2 model: adaptation to new bi-arm embodiments takes a few hours, typically using fewer than 200 examples. This is a reported adaptation result, not evidence of immediate deployment on a new body without additional data.

Together, these developer-reported results demonstrate relevant progress in manipulation, cross-embodiment transfer, grounded instruction following, and multi-step execution. Describing all of the achieved capability as short-horizon would understate the reported longer-task results. Nevertheless, the supplied review does not establish an independently scored evaluation of unfamiliar whole jobs over a defined shift, using an unchanged system without coaching or task-specific adaptation. It also does not establish that no other system has met that scope.

The evidence available here has specific limits. The supplied review used π0.7 text that ends within Appendix A-G; its relevant main-text passages and captions were available, but figure graphics and videos were not inspected. The DeepMind article's extracted text was complete, and the linked safety report supplied all 18 pages of text, but its figure graphics were not inspected. Numerical plot results therefore cannot be independently assessed from this record. The supplied freshness-search record is empty, leaving field-wide status as of 1 November 2026 unverified. These limitations constrain interpretation; they do not establish that the reported results are false.

completion_criteria.text: Proposed demonstration, not an established standard: an independent team evaluates one unchanged policy system in unfamiliar homes that the developers did not instrument. Ordinary-language goals specify finished jobs. The task suite includes clutter, articulated appliances, and at least one deformable object. Jobs last on the order of tens of minutes, and the suite explicitly includes recoverable execution errors so that autonomous recovery is tested rather than inferred from duration. Completion requires achieving the specified outcome without human coaching or resets between steps.
completion_criteria.label: Independent evaluation: unchanged policy completes unfamiliar home jobs without coaching or resets

completion_criteria.text: Proposed measurement and reproducibility requirements: before evaluation, specify task-selection procedures, success thresholds, intervention rules, and the duration of a shift of jobs. Report whole-job success, human interventions, failures, safety incidents, and whether recovery succeeded. Document the fixed system configuration, its training and adaptation exposure, and the basis for calling environments and jobs unfamiliar. Independent repetition across additional homes and task variations would make the result more convincing and help distinguish repeatable competence from favorable task selection.
completion_criteria.label: Pre-specify protocol and report whole-job outcomes, exposure, and unfamiliarity basis

completion_criteria.text: Proposed practical boundaries: report which objects, loads, appliance types, environmental conditions, and manipulation demands the demonstration covers. A resident's willingness to leave the robot unsupervised is an intended practical outcome, not a reproducible success threshold or a substitute for safety certification. Home results should support claims about their demonstrated scope; workplace competence requires corresponding workplace evaluations. No finite test suite can establish literal universality.
completion_criteria.label: Report covered scope without universality, workplace competence, or safety certification

related_concepts.text: Within the supplied roster, ROB-02, Autonomous dexterous tool use and in-hand manipulation at human reliability, concerns the quality and versatility of manipulation itself. ROB-01 concerns completing unfamiliar jobs, potentially using parallel-jaw grippers or simple hands where those suffice. Better dexterity could broaden its task range, but dependable instruction following does not establish a universal hand. ROB-07, Predictive contact mechanics that plans real manipulation, could supply better predictions for action selection and recovery; it addresses a supporting planning capability rather than the complete language-to-job system.

ROB-09, Lifelong on-robot learning that retains and composes physical skills, overlaps through skill composition and adaptation. ROB-01's proposed evaluation fixes the system and excludes per-task fine-tuning, whereas ROB-09 concerns acquiring and retaining capabilities over time. A robot could learn skills before an ROB-01 evaluation, but success on that evaluation would not by itself establish lifelong retention or learning without interference. Embodied common sense overlaps ROB-01 wherever choosing, sequencing, and repairing actions requires grounded reasoning; it is not a separate entry in the supplied roster.

ROB-03, An artificial muscle that can serve as the main actuator of a useful robot, concerns actuation hardware that could improve a robot's physical implementation. ROB-05, Load-bearing robotic matter that reforms into working machines, concerns reconfigurable material and machine structure. Neither is required by ROB-01's identity, and neither would by itself supply reliable instruction following or unfamiliar-job completion.

ROB-04, Closed-loop robotic self-reproduction from feedstock, and ROB-08, Robot collectives that build functional structures from bulk material, overlap with ROB-01 in autonomous sequencing and physical execution. Their defining outcomes are respectively reproduction and collective construction. Completing everyday jobs would not establish either outcome, and success at a specialized construction or reproduction process would not establish broad competence in unfamiliar homes.

ROB-06, Untethered intervention at a target inside the living human body, and ROB-10, Completion of full surgical procedures on living patients, concern distinct medical settings and outcomes. They can share requirements for perception, planning, manipulation, and recovery, but evidence from everyday environments cannot establish performance inside the body or competence to complete surgery. These entries remain separate from ROB-01.

change_log.change: Preserved ROB-01's identity while describing an unchanged policy system that may include a fixed hierarchy and auxiliary models.
change_log.reason: The target is system-level competence; requiring one monolithic controller would unnecessarily narrow the innovation.

change_log.change: Replaced categorical claims about present robots and field-wide absence with dated findings and a bounded account of what the supplied evidence establishes.
change_log.reason: The empty freshness record cannot establish the status of the entire field as of 1 November 2026.

change_log.change: Clarified π0.7's embodiment-specific laundry transfer and training exposure in specialist comparisons.
change_log.reason: Absence of laundry data from the target embodiment is narrower than absence of laundry training, and specialist-comparison tasks were represented in training.

change_log.change: Distinguished instruction-level scoring from whole-job reliability and retained the 3–6 instruction, four-kitchen, and two-bedroom details.
change_log.reason: The supplied caption supports those counts, but its metric does not establish extended autonomous job completion.

change_log.change: Added the high-level policy training that follows coaching for some unfamiliar longer π0.7 tasks.
change_log.reason: Autonomous execution after coaching-derived training does not meet the proposed unchanged-system, no-coaching criterion.

change_log.change: Separated Gemini Robotics 2's action checkpoint, embodied reasoning model, and On-Device 2 adaptation claim.
change_log.reason: Their reported capabilities and adaptation requirements apply to different components and should not be conflated.

change_log.change: Expanded the achieved-state account beyond short-horizon generalization and retained the evidence-access limitations.
change_log.reason: The sources report multi-step and longer-task progress, while incomplete extraction and uninspected graphics limit independent assessment.

change_log.change: Made recovery, whole-job scoring, intervention reporting, advance evaluation rules, and reproducibility explicit in the proposed demonstration.
change_log.reason: Duration and resident confidence alone do not provide a reproducible test of autonomous recovery or reliable completion.

change_log.change: Qualified workplace applications and the computation analogy, and separated competence from deployment economics, endurance, dexterity, and safety.
change_log.reason: A home demonstration would support a bounded capability claim rather than universal labor competence or deployment readiness.

change_log.change: Explained relationships across the supplied roster without merging entries.
change_log.reason: Shared components do not erase differences in physical capability, learning regime, operating environment, or required outcome.

unresolved_issues: Whether any system had demonstrated the full proposed capability by 1 November 2026 remains unverified because the supplied freshness-search record is empty.
The degree of novelty of π0.7's test instructions remains difficult to quantify; the supplied material does not resolve task-level independence from training exposure.
The π0.7 extraction ends within Appendix A-G, and figure graphics and videos were not inspected in the supplied review. Additional numerical or visual conclusions cannot be resolved from this record.
The proposed evaluation still requires concrete choices for task sampling, shift duration, success thresholds, intervention rules, and reproducibility procedures; these are not established standards.
The task and environment breadth needed to justify unsupervised use, and the separate safety and economic requirements for deployment, remain open.
